content: Early identification and treatment of lower respiratory tract infections are critical in managing lung disease in individuals with cystic fibrosis (CF). When sputum samples cannot be obtained, diagnosis typically relies on cultures from oropharyngeal specimens. However, there are concerns regarding the sensitivity of this method in detecting organisms present in the lower respiratory tract. Bronchoscopy, along with procedures like bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL), is invasive but allows for the collection of specimens directly from the lower respiratory tract in patients who do not produce sputum. Cultures obtained from bronchoscopic specimens yield a higher number of organisms compared to those from oropharyngeal specimens. Regular use of bronchoscopy and related procedures may enhance the accuracy of diagnosing lower respiratory tract infections and improve antimicrobial selection, potentially leading to clinical benefits. This review updates previous versions published in 2013, 2016, and 2018. The objective of this review was to assess the effectiveness of bronchoscopy-guided antimicrobial therapy in managing lung infections in both adults and children with CF. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted in the Cochrane Cystic Fibrosis Trials Register, which includes data from electronic databases, journal handsearching, and conference abstracts. Additional searches were performed in three registries of ongoing studies and reference lists of relevant articles. The most recent search was completed on November 1, 2023. The review included randomized controlled trials involving CF patients of any age. These trials compared outcomes of antimicrobial therapies guided by bronchoscopy (and related procedures) with those guided by other sampling methods, such as sputum cultures, throat swabs, or cough swabs. Two independent reviewers selected studies, assessed their risk of bias, and extracted data. Study investigators were contacted for additional information when necessary. The certainty of the evidence was evaluated using the GRADE criteria. Two studies were included in this updated review. The first study involved 170 infants under six months of age diagnosed with CF through newborn screening. Participants were followed until the age of five, with data available for 157 children. This study compared pulmonary exacerbation outcomes between BAL-directed treatment and standard treatment based on clinical features and oropharyngeal cultures. The second study included 30 children aged 5 to 18 years with CF. Participants were randomized to receive treatment based on microbiological results of BAL triggered by an increase in lung clearance index (LCI) of at least one unit above baseline or standard treatment based on microbiological results of oropharyngeal samples collected during symptomatic episodes. Both studies were judged to have a low risk of bias in most domains, although the smaller study had unclear risks for allocation concealment and selective reporting. In the larger study, the statistical power to detect a significant difference in the prevalence of Pseudomonas aeruginosa was low because the isolation rates of Pseudomonas aeruginosa in BAL samples at five years of age were much lower than anticipated during power calculations. The certainty of evidence for key outcomes was graded as low, except for high-resolution computed tomography (CT) scoring and cost-of-care analysis, which were graded as moderate certainty. The two studies reported similar outcomes, but meta-analysis was not feasible due to differences in outcome measurement methods and indications for BAL use. Evidence suggests that BAL-directed antimicrobial therapy may make little or no difference in lung function z-scores after two years, as measured by changes in LCI and forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) (low-certainty evidence). At five years, the larger study found little or no difference in absolute FEV1 z-scores or forced vital capacity (FVC) (low-certainty evidence). BAL-directed therapy likely has minimal or no impact on chest CT scores at two or five years (moderate-certainty evidence). It may also have little or no effect on nutritional parameters or the number of positive Pseudomonas aeruginosa isolates per participant per year but may result in more hospitalizations per year (low-certainty evidence). There was likely no difference in average care costs per participant, including hospitalizations and total costs, at five years between BAL-directed therapy and standard care (moderate-certainty evidence). No differences were observed in health-related quality of life between BAL-directed therapy and standard care at two or five years. The larger study also found no difference in the number of Pseudomonas aeruginosa isolates per child per year. Eradication rates following one or two courses of eradication treatment and the number of pulmonary exacerbations were similar between the two groups. Mild adverse events, when reported, were generally well tolerated, with transient worsening of cough being the most common, occurring after 29% of procedures. Significant clinical deterioration was documented during or within 24 hours of BAL in 4.8% of procedures. In conclusion, this review, which included two well-designed randomized controlled studies, found no evidence to support the routine use of BAL for diagnosing and managing pulmonary infections in preschool children with CF compared to standard care based on oropharyngeal culture results and clinical symptoms. No evidence is currently available for adults.
